At this point, the functional purity of iterating methods, unfortunately, ends.

A function can mutate an object by reference.

In this case, as a rule, **side effects** occur.
s3.p4: There are two ways to pass references in array iterating methods.
s3.p5: The first one is passing a reference to the **call context** of the **function-argument** by the second argument of the method.
s3.p6: The second is passing the reference to the source array to the **function-argument** itself when calling it.

s6.p1: ![ico-20 warn] Pure functions, as iterative methods are supposed to be, do not generate **side effects**, i.e. no _external variables are mutated_.
s6.p2: Array iterating methods are **higher-order functions** that iterate over a source array, passing one array element at a time as an argument to the function.
s6.p3: Thus, the **function-argument** does not have a reference to the original array itself, and cannot mutate it.
s6.p4: ![ico-20 warn] Except the cases when the elements of the source array have a reference data type, i.e. The function-argument receives not a value but a reference to an array element.
s6.p5: The original array, as a rule, does not change.
s6.p6: That is, they were originally supposed to be **pure functions** that do not generate external effects, which distinguishes them from ordinary array methods such as ⟦f18⟧, ⟦f19⟧, etc.
s6.p7: But we have already shown earlier that this functional purity is violated by passing references (the reference to the call context of function-argument or the reference to the source array).
s6.p8: Similarly, if we are dealing with **deep data structures**, then it is not values ​​that are passed, but references, which creates the possibility of **side effects**.

s7.p1: If a method every time being called returns the same result with the same argument values, then it is **_idempotent_**.
s7.p2: ^^i.e. when calling a method with the same array and function repeatedly, the result will always be the same.^^
s7.p3: In object-oriented languages, method idempotency is practically unattainable if the function arguments have a **reference data type**.
s7.p4: Because arrays have a **reference data type**, array iterating methods operate with a reference.
s7.p5: The reference remains the same, but from one method call to the next, the contents of the array may have changed, which will affect the result.
